paragraphs.text: See 2Ki 21:1.
paragraphs.anchor: Manasseh was twelve years old.

paragraphs.text: So long he reigned, (1.) For the punishment of the people’s sins; (2.) That he might have time enough to amend his own life; (3.) That in him, as afterwards in Paul, "God might show forth all longsuffering, for a pattern to them who should afterwards believe on him to life everlasting." {1Ti 1:16} Vide ubi supra.
paragraphs.anchor: And he reigned fifty and five years.

paragraphs.text: He quickly made mad Work, as we say, turning all upside down. So great is the loss of good princes, when they die: and so suddenly can God cause the sun to go down over a nation, even at noonday, for the just punishment of such ungrateful wretches as love darkness better than light, because their works are evil. See on 2Ki 21:2.
paragraphs.anchor: But he did that which was evil.

paragraphs.text: Heb., He returned, and built. He returned, but not to God. Whilst his father lived, he seemed to hate the high places; but now he changed his mind, but for the worse: profecit in peius. See 2Ki 21:3.
paragraphs.anchor: For he built again.

paragraphs.text: So do those, after a sort, that attribute to the stars more than is meet.
paragraphs.anchor: He worshipped all the host of heaven.

paragraphs.text: Which was as bad as for a wife to bring her paramours into her husband’s bed.
paragraphs.anchor: In the house of the Lord.

paragraphs.text: See 2Ki 21:5.
paragraphs.anchor: And he built altars.

paragraphs.text: Thinking thereby to merit remission of sin, {Mic 6:7} and to obtain victories, as that king of Moab did. {2Ki 3:27}
paragraphs.anchor: And he caused his children to pass, &c.

paragraphs.text: Five of those six sorts of witchcraft mentioned by Moses, {Deu 18:9-14} Manasseh fell into. See 2Ki 21:6.
paragraphs.anchor: And he observed times, and used enchantments.

paragraphs.text: This was some special idol worshipped by him in a grove, and now brought into the temple, as it were on purpose to provoke the Lord. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: The idol which he had made.

See 2Ki 21:8.
paragraphs.anchor: Neither will I any more.

paragraphs.text: The people follow their prince, as in a beast the body followoth the head: and as in a fish, putrefaction beginneth at the head: so here.
paragraphs.anchor: So Manasseh made Judah.

paragraphs.text: sc., By his prophets, Isaiah, Joel, Micah, Habakkuk, and others; sed surdo fabulam; they lost their sweet words.
paragraphs.anchor: And the Lord spake to Manasseh

paragraphs.text: Manasseh, though son to good Hezekiah, and one of our Saviour’s progenitors, was not spared; and shall other such sinners go unpunished? Never think it.
paragraphs.anchor: Wherefore the Lord brought upon them.

paragraphs.text: Of the king of Babylon, saith Josephus: but herein, saith Lyra, there is no difference. Assyria was the beginning of the Babylonish monarchy.
paragraphs.anchor: Of the king of Assyria.

paragraphs.text: Or, Thistles, as 2Ki 14:9. Thither he had now fled to hide himself, who erst had faced the heavens, and opposed with crest and breast whatsoever stood in the way of his sins and lusts. The prophet Isaiah he had sawn asunder, if all be true that is storied of him. Now himself was carried bound to Babylon, and there put into a brazen vessel full of holes, saith Jerome, and therein tormented by fire put about it. At other times he was fed, saith Chrysostom, {a} but with so much barley bread in a day, and so much water mingled with vinegar, as might keep him alive: being all the while bound with chains in the prison house, and this of itself was misery enough for a king to endure. We know the proverb, Si non sis qui fueris, non est cur velis vivere.
paragraphs.anchor: Which took Manasseh among the thorns.

paragraphs.text: {a} Hom. i. in Matt,

When the rod spake, he heard it {Mic 6:9} who would not hear the word. {2Ch 33:10} God sent him into the dungeon to repent; as he did David into the depths, and Jonah into the whale’s belly to pray. Adversity hath whipt many a soul to heaven, which otherwise prosperity had coached to hell.
paragraphs.anchor: And when he was in affliction.

paragraphs.text: There is a prayer extant that is said to be his, pia sane et elegans, saith Lavater; but it is Apocryphal, as not found in the Hebrew text.
paragraphs.anchor: He besought the Lord.

paragraphs.text: As he had sinned greatly, so his humiliation bore a proportion, being deep, downright, and such as brought him home. The prodigal changed many places ere he came home in earnest. Many came out of Egypt, that never came into Canaan. Ahab humbled himself, so did those justiciaries, {Isa 58:3} but not greatly, as Manasseh; their sorrow for sin was but skin deep.
paragraphs.anchor: And humbled himself greatly.

paragraphs.text: His afflictions, like Benhadad’s best counsellors, sent Manasseh with a cord about his neck, to the merciful King of Israel.
paragraphs.anchor: And prayed to him.

paragraphs.text: Note this against those old and our new Novatians. Despair not of mercy, though never so sinful; but know, that if men can find a praying heart, God will find a pitying heart.
paragraphs.anchor: And he was entreated of him, and heard his supplication.

paragraphs.text: How, and by what means, is not recorded. The Lord knoweth how to deliver his. {2Pe 2:9}
paragraphs.anchor: And brought him again to Jerusalem.

paragraphs.text: This lesson he had learned in the school of BabyIon. Christianorum Theologia, Crux, saith Luther. The cross had taught Manasseh more of God than ever he knew before.
paragraphs.anchor: Then Manasseh knew that the Lord he was God.

paragraphs.text: It is uncertain how he got out of prison; whether with the king of Babylon’s good leave, or by making escape. There are that tell us, that the prison doors were opened, his chains loosened, and he delivered, as afterwards Peter was. {Act 12:3-11} Howsoever, he thought good to fortify himself against the Babylonians, and whatsoever enemies. This, though it be here set down first, yet Josephus saith, that the first work he did after his return, was to reform religion.
paragraphs.anchor: Now after this he built a wall.

paragraphs.text: This he had promised to do, doubtless, in his distress; and now he doth it. "Vow, and perform to the Lord your God," &c.
paragraphs.anchor: And he took away the strange gods.

paragraphs.text: Saying unto them, "Get you hence." {Isa 30:22} "What have I to do any more with idols?" {Hos 14:8} This was his repentance from sin.
paragraphs.anchor: And cast them out of the city.

paragraphs.text: Which himself had defaced in his idolatrous humour. His contrition was seconded with conversion; his humiliation with reformation.
paragraphs.anchor: And he repaired the altar of the Lord.

paragraphs.text: Before he had seduced them, now he reduceth them into the right way; laying God’s and his charge upon them to live better.
paragraphs.anchor: And commanded Judah to serve the Lord

paragraphs.text: Do Manasseh what he could to the contrary. Plus valet malum inolitum, quam bonum insolitum. It is hard to break people off their sinful and superstitious customs.
paragraphs.anchor: Nevertheless the people did sacrifice.

paragraphs.text: See on 2Ch 33:12.
paragraphs.anchor: And his prayer unto God.

paragraphs.text: Which was sure some excellent and eximious prayer, and is therefore so much mentioned. Affliction exciteth devotion: and then, if ever, men "pray in the Holy Ghost."
paragraphs.anchor: His prayer also

paragraphs.text: His transgression against God, and his trespass against men. So St Paul, I was - as to the first table - "a blasphemer," saith he, and - as to the second - "a persecutor": and - as to both - "injurious," one that wronged both God and man. {1Ti 1:13}
paragraphs.anchor: And all his sin, and his trespass.

paragraphs.text: Or, Of Hosai, who might be some prophet, whose book is not now extant. Some Rabbis hold that Hosai is Isaiah. Others of them say, that Isaiah was slain by Manasseh, before his captivity. Seder Olam maketh mention of Ozai as a prophet under the reign of Amon.
paragraphs.anchor: Among the sayings of the seers.

paragraphs.text: Twelve, saith the Greeks. Perhaps he reigned ten years in his father’s absence, as Philo saith he did.
